The American shrew mole (Neurotrichus gibbsii) exhibits a distinct set of life-history traits that align with its fossorial and semi-aquatic habits within the Talpidae. At a stable body temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], males and females become reproductively mature at approximately 250 days since birth [tp = approximately 250 days since birth], a timing that appears linked to the constraints of their energetically demanding burrowing lifestyle. Neonates emerge from the reproductive tract after a gestation period that averages 28 days [tg = 28 days] under these same thermoregulatory conditions of 35 °C, which is typical for small insectivorous mammals of this size at a temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. The brevity of uterine development, ranging from 21 to 30 days in published accounts, reflects a pattern of altricial young born in an underdeveloped state. Newborn individuals weigh a mere 0.9 grams [Wwb = 0.9 grams] at parturition, a minimal mass that underscores the high degree of maternal investment required during the subsequent suckling period.

Weaning in the American shrew mole represents a critical transition to nutritional independence, occurring at 17 days after birth [tx = 17 days after birth] when pups are maintained at a core temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. This relatively short lactation period is characteristic of small mammals that produce altricial offspring in secure subterranean nests, where predation risk is low and the mother can afford frequent nursing bouts. During this pre-weaning phase, the suckling juveniles are entirely dependent on milk for their rapid growth, gaining body mass steadily before they begin to consume invertebrate prey. The age at weaning is notably early when compared to other members of the Talpidae, suggesting a strategy that prioritizes rapid development in a thermally buffered environment. After the dietary transition to solid food, the young animals continue to grow within the natal nest for a brief period before dispersing to establish their own burrow systems in the moist forest soils they prefer.

The species attains a maximum recorded lifespan of approximately 1004 days [am = approximately 1004 days] when measured under the controlled thermoneutral conditions of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], a value that positions Neurotrichus gibbsii as a relatively short-lived mammal within its body size range. This longevity estimate, equivalent to roughly 2.75 years, corresponds well with field mark-recapture studies that indicate few individuals survive beyond their third breeding season. The comparatively brief life expectancy is likely influenced by the high energetic costs of constant burrowing activity and the metabolic demands of maintaining a stable body temperature in cool, damp substrates. Senescence appears to set in rapidly after the second year, with a marked decline in physical condition and foraging efficiency noted among older adults in captive colonies. Natural mortality from predation and environmental stress acts as a powerful selective force, favoring early and intense reproductive effort over extended somatic maintenance.

Under the same thermal regime of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], the basal metabolic rate of the American shrew mole has been measured at 46.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 46.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that reflects the high energy turnover typical of small insectivores with active lifestyles. This resting oxygen consumption is substantially elevated when compared to similarly sized rodents, likely as an adaptation to the metabolically demanding tasks of digging tunnel networks and swimming through watercourses in search of prey. The elevated metabolic machinery supports a life history characterized by rapid growth and early maturation, but it also imposes a constant need for high-quality invertebrate food resources. Field observations suggest that individuals must consume a significant portion of their body weight in prey daily to meet these energetic requirements. The metabolic rate recorded under laboratory conditions provides a useful benchmark for understanding the physiological constraints that shape the species' ecology.

Reproductive output in the American shrew mole is constrained by a slow reproductive frequency; females typically produce a single litter each year [F_R_i = single litter each year], with litter sizes of one to four pups per litter [N_R_i = one to four pups per litter] occurring at a maternal thermoneutral temperature of 35.8 °C [T = 35.8 °C]. This annual reproductive rate, yielding only a handful of offspring per breeding season, is among the lowest recorded for North American soricomorphs of comparable body size. The reduced fecundity is offset by intensive maternal care during the gestation and lactation periods, which together occupy a substantial fraction of the annual cycle. Adult body mass in reproductively active individuals typically stabilizes around 10 grams [Wwi = around 10 grams], although published accounts from the Animal Diversity Web document a broader range of 8 to 14.5 grams depending on seasonal food availability and geographic locality. This ultimate wet weight reflects the moderate size of this mole relative to its fossorial relatives.
